title: Decoding Lung Cancer with Artificial Intelligence: A Path to Personalized Diagnostics and Therapy.
source: PubMed · Journal of environmental pathology, toxicology and oncology : official organ of the International Society for Environmental Toxicology and Cancer
desc: [Journal of environmental pathology, toxicology and oncology : official organ of the International Society for Environmental Toxicology and Cancer] Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents the majority of lung cancer cases and remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Early detection, accurate staging, and individualized therapy are crucial for improving patient survival. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed NSCLC care through the automated analysis of imaging, pathology, and molecular datasets. Deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high accuracy in tumor detection, histologic classification, biomarker prediction (PD-L1, EGFR, KRAS) and prognosis assessment. Integration of the AI with whole slide imaging (WSI), computed tomography (CT), PET/CT and liquid biopsies enables non-invasive tumor characterization, early recurrence detection and prediction of treatment response. Multimodal AI approaches that combine imaging, genomic, and clinical data offer superior patient stratification and personalized treatment planning compared with traditional methods. Beyond diagnosis, AI facilitates therapeutic development through radiomics based nodule classification, multi-omics data interpretation, and drug discovery. Radiomics, in particular, extracts quantitative imaging biomarkers that capture tumor heterogeneity beyond human perception. The AI further supports clinical decision-making in surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, enhancing workflow efficiency. Despite challenges in data quality, interpretability, and clinical adoption, AI holds significant promise for advancing precision oncology and improving outcomes in NSCLC management.

title: MATS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Controllable and Reflective Tumor Synthesis
desc: Synthesizing realistic tumors on medical images helps address data scarcity for clinical AI. Existing diffusion-based methods, however, lack fine-grained attribute-level controllability, closed-loop quality verification, and awareness of which morphological patterns are underrepresented in the target distribution. We present MATS, a multi-agent framework for text-controllable, cross-organ tumor synthesis. Given a target disease, MATS first profiles its morphological distribution over a fine-grained attribute space covering tumor geometry and appearance, and constructs a generation plan that amplifies underrepresented subtypes while keeping common ones dominant. It then localizes the target organ, proposes anatomically valid placement, and executes two-stage diffusion to produce the tumor mask and render texture, each conditioned on the corresponding attributes. A closed-loop reflective mechanism verifies attribute alignment at three checkpoints throughout synthesis and provides targeted feedback to guide re-generation when misalignment is detected. Trained exclusively on a single-source pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor dataset, MATS consistently improves downstream segmentation both in-domain and across LiTS, KiTS, and MSD-Pancreas benchmarks, whereas most prior generative augmentation methods fall below real-only training.

title: Algorithmic design choices as determinants of health equity: a causal simulation study of healthcare resource allocation
desc: Background. Care management programs increasingly rely on prediction algorithms to decide which patients receive limited healthcare resources. Because these algorithms are typically trained to predict future healthcare utilization or cost, they may systematically underidentify patients whose care-seeking behavior is suppressed by structural barriers. Objective. To evaluate how three modifiable design choices (selection threshold, feature set, and training objective) affect allocation equity in care management targeting. Methods. We constructed an analytical cohort of 201,216 adults from linked electronic health record and participant survey data in the NIH All of Us Research Program (2017-2019). Three prediction models (logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost) were trained and evaluated under simulation conditions that varied one design choice at a time while holding the others fixed. Equity was assessed using false negative rate (FNR), equal opportunity difference (EOD), and allocation rate conditional on need (an access-independent benchmark based on self-reported general health status). We also applied Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to identify which predictors contributed most to the Black-White allocation gap. Results. Prior utilization understated self-reported health burden among disadvantaged groups: 33% of Black and 32% of Hispanic participants reported fair or poor health, yet only 22% and 19% were classified as high utilizers. White participants showed the opposite pattern: 25% were classified as high utilizers, while only 19% reported fair or poor general health status. Under baseline design choices, all three models produced similar disparities, with uninsured participants showing the largest gap (EOD: -0.148). Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition identified prior outpatient visits as the dominant contributor to the Black-White gap in predicted allocation, with higher average emergency department utilization among Black participants partially offsetting the effect. Varying the selection threshold had little effect; disparities persisted across all thresholds. Feature set variation produced mixed and group-specific effects; removal of prior outpatient visits achieved near-zero Black-White EOD (0.001, AUC: 0.77), consistent with the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition finding. Training objective variation produced the most substantial and consistent equity effects, with the health status objective achieving near-zero Black-White EOD (0.008, AUC: 0.69) an

title: FateDriver: Weakly supervised dual-view graph learning for transition-specific prioritization of candidate regulators in cellular reprogramming
desc: Cellular reprogramming supports regenerative medicine, yet the endogenous regulators of a specified source-to-target transition remain incompletely defined. Existing computational methods rank candidate regulators from network topology, trajectory dynamics, or cell-state labels, leaving unused the factors experimentally delivered to induce the transition. We present FateDriver, a weakly supervised dual-view graph neural network that jointly represents cells and genes from single-cell transcriptomes, treats the delivered factors as sparse gene-level labels, and ranks the remaining genes for a specified transition under a positive--unlabeled formulation. Across two OSKM datasets and one GMT dataset, FateDriver ranked first or second among six methods in recovering externally curated reference genes, exceeded a supervision-matched non-graph model despite weaker co-expression with the delivered factors, and achieved the highest recovery of protein targets of pluripotency-inducing chemical cocktails in both OSKM datasets. Holding either the source or the endpoint fixed yielded distinct candidate programs, including a DDX58--interferon axis associated with cells lacking endogenous pluripotency markers. Applying the same framework to candidate source--target pairs prioritized distinct candidate origins for two in vivo partially reprogrammed intestinal populations. FateDriver converts sparse experimental knowledge into transition-specific hypotheses for regulator prioritization from single-cell trajectories.

title: An update on combinational chemo-immunotherapy for breast cancer using nanotechnology.
source: PubMed · Expert opinion on drug delivery
desc: [Expert opinion on drug delivery] Breast cancer is still a considerable public health issue worldwide. However, earlier studies reported that chemotherapeutic drugs suppress the immune system. Therefore, a combination of chemotherapeutic agents with an immunomodulator might enhance antitumor immunity through immunogenic cell death, cross-priming, and the regulation of immune checkpoint molecules. Nanotechnology-enabled drug delivery has received considerable attention in chemo-immunotherapy. A comprehensive literature review was performed using google scholar, Science Direct, the Clinical Research Database, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and DOAJ. The review discusses the combination of immunotherapy and nanotechnology including AI-based techniques used to identify suitable biomarkers and to enable selective drug delivery to breast cancer cells. The combinational therapy containing chemotherapeutic agents and immunomodulators has shown promising results due to their synergistic effects. The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in nanomedicine has enabled the design of nanoparticles, predict their interactions with drugs, and personalize treatment based on patients' individual tumor profiles. This advancement has marked the advent of precision medicine in oncology, which focuses on tailoring therapies to each tumor's molecular and genetic profile. Despite these encouraging developments, several challenges remain in nanotechnology for cancer therapy, including mass production, biosafety, regulatory issues, and the successful translation of laboratory findings into clinical practice.

title: Can Personal Requirements Become Supervision for Planning?
desc: Managing multiple chronic conditions through diet requires satisfying disease- and medication-specific requirements jointly across meals and days while preserving established eating habits. These requirements are public in clinical guidelines and drug labels, yet turning them into a feasible plan for one person remains difficult for language-model agents. In our dietitian-approved weekly planning evaluation built from NHANES, thirteen models, from medically fine-tuned 8B models to GPT-6.1 Sol, pass fewer than 3% of complete plans through direct generation. Explicit rules, higher reasoning effort, or model-directed tools leave GPT-6.1 Sol at no more than 8%. We present Noura, which pairs LLM planning with executable personal specifications instantiated from public clinical guidance and individual health and dietary profiles. During planning, the specification grounds foods, optimizes portions, checks the complete multi-day plan, and guides revision. Our key insight is that a specification that rejects a plan can also determine what to learn from it. Noura turns executed plans and contextually credited revisions into supervision for compact models, recovering targets even from trajectories that never achieve complete success. The same specification supplies supervised targets, preferences, and rewards for post-training. On 4,993 held-out participants, Noura-SFT raises Qwen3-14B's complete-plan pass rate from 24.0% to 72.5% within the same execution loop, cuts rule violations by 97.5% with no observed critical failures, and improves dietary quality. The locally hosted 14B planner incurs fewer rule violations than its GPT-6 Luna teacher. A matched comparison shows that executed targets reduce rule violations by 41% over model-written proposals. Across four Qwen, Phi, and Llama backbones, self-training alone reduces rule violations by 41-61% on a 1,249-person population subset.

title: Interpreting graph neural networks reveals microbial association patterns in inflammatory bowel diseases
desc: Traditional machine learning models trained on gut microbiome abundance profiles can distinguish individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from non-IBD individuals. However, their interpretation typically considers taxa in isolation, making it difficult to understand how associations between taxa contribute to predictions. Here, we inferred individual-specific microbial association networks from longitudinal metagenomics data of 106 individuals in HMP2/iHMP and used them to train and interpret graph neural network (GNN) models, which we compared with abundance-based models such as Random Forest (RF). Although RF achieved higher predictive performance (AUPRC ~0.59 vs 0.446), interpreting the GNNs revealed that their predictions relied on a densely connected module of co-abundant Bacteroidales species. Unlike the taxa prioritized by RF, these species were not differentially abundant between conditions. In an independent cohort, this module carried most of the predictive signal, and removing its associations reduced performance to near chance. These results show that coordinated association structure, rather than abundance shifts alone, is a feature of the IBD gut microbiome, and that interpreting GNNs can uncover such patterns that complement abundance-based analyses.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Facelift Surgery: A Systematic Review of Objective Outcome Assessment and Patient-Perceived Rejuvenation.
desc: [Aesthetic plastic surgery] Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a tool for objective outcome assessment in facelift surgery (rhytidectomy), yet the clinical validity and limitations of these technologies remain incompletely characterized. This review evaluates the evidence on AI applications in facelift surgery, focusing on neural network based age estimation, concordance with patient perception, and large language model (LLM) supported patient counseling. A systematic review was conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Databases were searched for studies applying AI to facelift surgery with primary clinical data. Nine studies published between 2020 and 2025 met inclusion criteria. Convolutional neural networks quantified postoperative age reduction ranging from 1.7 to 5.8 years depending on surgical technique and follow-up interval. AI-derived estimates consistently underestimated patient-perceived rejuvenation by approximately 35% to 50%. Superficial musculoaponeurotic system-based techniques demonstrated greater AI-measured age reduction than skin-only procedures. LLMs achieved 85% to 88% diagnostic accuracy for patient counseling but exceeded recommended readability standards. AI enables objective quantification of facelift outcomes but demonstrates systematic discordance with patient perception. Current AI modalities should function as adjuncts to validated patient-reported outcome measures, not replacements. These preliminary findings warrant cautious interpretation given the limited and heterogeneous evidence base. Ethical concerns regarding algorithmic definitions of surgical success warrant consideration. This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 .

title: LAPIS: Clinically Constrained Patient-Identity Residual Learning for Chest X-Ray Anonymization
desc: Biometric information in chest radiographs limits their release for research, as patients can be re-identified. We propose LAPIS, which jointly adapts a spatial chest-radiograph latent space so that patient-discriminative information concentrates in a compact, replaceable channel residual while most clinically relevant content stays in the complement. The residual is defined by an exactly semi-orthogonal basis, a spatial adversary suppresses identity leakage from the complement, and replacement-aware training teaches the decoder cross-patient residual swaps under output identity, clinical and realism constraints, so that replacing the residual yields a valid image. At release, the residual is replaced by a mixture of donor residuals. On patient-disjoint model, release and test sets from ChestX-ray14, we evaluate attackers adapted to the anonymized setting, a structural source-retrieval attack, and pathology classifiers trained on released images and tested on real ones. LAPIS reduces worst-case cross-study linkability from 0.961 to 0.791 AUC at a macro AUROC cost of 0.012 relative to reconstruction; a deformation-based baseline, however, remains better at structural source retrieval.

title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS
desc: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

Advances in artificial intelligence-driven MRI research in Alzheimer's disease.
desc: [Frontiers in neurology] Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, poses substantial challenges for early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring-two cornerstones of effective clinical management and therapeutic intervention. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), owing to its non-invasiveness and high spatial resolution, has emerged as an indispensable tool in AD research. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) techniques, has demonstrated remarkable potential for automating MRI analysis, extracting subtle imaging features, and supporting objective disease prediction. This review comprehensively summarizes the latest advances in AI-driven MRI applications for AD diagnosis, staging, prognosis, and adjuvant therapeutic monitoring. It highlights key progress in AI model development, multimodal data processing, and clinical translational value. Furthermore, current bottlenecks, including data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and real-world deployment, are systematically discussed, and future directions are outlined to enhance the precision and clinical utility of AI-assisted MRI in AD. Overall, AI-MRI has evolved from laboratory validation toward early clinical adoption, with explainability and multi-center generalizability identified as critical priorities in the next research phase.

title: Zonal-Aware Prostate Cancer Detection and Classification via Hadamard-Fused Mamba-UNet
desc: Accurate clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection from prostate MRI requires a detailed understanding of the prostate anatomical context. Deep learning approaches have achieved promising results in zonal and lesion segmentation; however, the joint analysis of prostate zonal anatomy and lesion morphology in a unified framework remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we propose ZH-Mamba, a multi-stage zonal-aware csPCa detection framework consisting of two H-Mamba UNets models for prostate zonal segmentation and lesion localization, followed by an anatomy-aware Convolutional Neural Network classifier for csPCa detection. The proposed model leverages a learnable Hadamard Transform-based fusion mechanism to enhance zonal and lesion feature representations without increasing computational complexity. The learned fusion patterns consistently emphasize prostate regions, suggesting that the proposed fusion captures anatomically relevant feature representations. We demonstrate a strong zonal segmentation performance on the PI-CAI dataset, reaching Dice scores of $\textbf{0.95}$, $\textbf{0.85}$, and $\textbf{0.95}$ for whole gland (WG), peripheral zone (PZ), and transition zone (TZ), respectively, providing robust anatomical priors for downstream csPCa detection. Experimental results on an independent internal dataset confirm the generalization capability of the proposed zonal segmentation model. For lesion localization, the H-Mamba UNet achieves a competitive Dice score of $\textbf{0.70}$. Integrating the zonal masks and lesion localization, the proposed ZH-Mamba framework achieves an AUC of $\textbf{0.86}$, Average Precision ($\mathrm{AP}_{\mathrm{Patient}}$) of $\textbf{0.72}$, and F1 score of $\textbf{0.76}$, demonstrating the effectiveness of zonal-aware csPCa detection.

title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
desc: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) of lung cancer. Approach: We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal CT dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the DIRLAB 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk (OAR) contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13,289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient. Main results: On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of \qty{1.8}{\mm}/\qty{2.8}{\mm} on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus \qty{1.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.4}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{2.1}{\mm}/\qty{3.0}{\mm} for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of \qty{3.9}{\mm}/\qty{2.6}{\mm} and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (\qty{3.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.7}{\mm}, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (\qty{4.4}{\mm}/\qty{2.9}{\mm}, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of \qty{1.74}{\mm}/\qty{0.30}{\mm} on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus \qty{2.41}{\mm}/\qty{0.56}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{6.65}{\mm}/\qty{3.92}{\mm} for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct GTV boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty. Significance: TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Segment Anything Pancreas: A Unified MRI Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Cancer Radiotherapy
desc: Background: Limited tumor annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumors and organs at risk (OARs) for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Purpose: We propose Pancreas-MedNeXt, a unified model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, tumors, and surrounding OARs from one MRI volume. Methods: The model uses a shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion pretraining, followed by multitask fine-tuning. Three output heads predict the pancreatic subregions, tumor, and OARs (stomach, duodenum, kidneys). An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labeled data without treating unannotated structures as background. Pancreas and tumor were evaluated by three-fold cross-validation on 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac), subregions and OARs on Cyst-X and AMOS test sets, and pancreas and OARs on 33 external T1-weighted TotalSegmentator scans. Comparisons with nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D, and Swin UNETR used the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Pancreas-MedNeXt achieved the highest mean pancreas and tumor DSC on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI. Tumor DSC was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 (95% CI: 0.28-9.45) and 5.89 (95% CI: 2.37-9.72) percentage points, respectively. Whole-pancreas DSC was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body, and tail DSC by 2.01, 3.00, and 3.78 percentage points over training from scratch. It also achieved the highest DSC for the pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney on AMOS, and for all five organs on external MRI, exceeding the next-best method by 4.92-8.85 percentage points.Conclusion: A single Pancreas-MedNeXt model segments tumors, pancreatic subregions, and OARs on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

title: Bioactivity foundation model for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization from sequence data
desc: Learning from large-scale bioactivity archives is complicated by heterogeneous assay readouts and differences in data reliability. Here we show that a model that predicts probability distributions over binding affinities from sequence data opens model training to vast and diverse troves of heterogeneous bioactivity data. We develop PSICHIC+, a bioactivity foundation model trained on approximately 82 million protein-ligand records using a distributional objective that preserves quantitative resolution while incorporating variation in data reliability. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, PSICHIC+ predicts binding affinity in milliseconds. In zero-shot virtual-screening benchmarks without target-specific training data, it improves enrichment over regression- and classification-based approaches and performs competitively with leading structure-based methods. In lab-in-the-loop campaigns, distribution-guided acquisition improves recovery of high-activity compounds under fixed screening budgets. Combining PSICHIC+ with Boltz-2 improves hit-to-lead affinity prediction over Boltz-2 alone, with mean correlation approaching that of FEP+ on the evaluated benchmarks, without requiring high-resolution protein structures. These results support distributional learning as a scalable approach to using heterogeneous bioactivity data for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization.

Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases.
desc: [Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine] Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.

title: CAMEL: Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning for Ultra-Lightweight Retinal Foundation Models
desc: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.

title: Andrew Dunn

Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review.
desc: [Frontiers in human neuroscience] Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

title: CS-LDM: Clinically Guided Structure-Aware Latent Diffusion for Knee Radiographic Forecasting
desc: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of physical disability and currently has no curative clinical treatment. Early diagnosis and accurate prognosis are therefore vital for managing its progression. Existing methods mainly predict future severity grades and provide limited visual explanation of structural change. Recent generation-guided approaches synthesize follow-up radiographs for progression assessment, but generated images are often judged by predictive accuracy or image realism, so they may satisfy a grading model while remaining morphologically unreliable. We therefore propose CS-LDM, a clinically guided, structure-aware latent diffusion framework that forecasts patient-specific future knee radiographs from the current X-ray and clinically available current KL grade, using LoRA adaptation, current-grade conditioning, and frozen-teacher diagnostic distillation. Experiments on the public Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset show that CS-LDM improves future severity-grade consistency while maintaining competitive image fidelity. Further ordinal, OARSI, ROI-level, and stable/progressed analyses show that radiographic forecasting should be evaluated by balancing diagnostic consistency, anatomical plausibility, and structural preservation.

title: Bracco invests $230M in first US diagnostic imaging manufacturing facility

PSMA Theranostics for Prostate Cancer: Evidence, Pitfalls, and Implementation in Japan.
source: PubMed · International journal of urology : official journal of the Japanese Urological Association
desc: [International journal of urology : official journal of the Japanese Urological Association] Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a Type II transmembrane glycoprotein markedly overexpressed on prostate cancer cells, enabling a single molecular target to support both positron emission tomography (PET) imaging and targeted radionuclide therapy. Over the past decade, PSMA-PET/CT has been incorporated into international guidelines for primary staging of high-risk prostate cancer and for biochemical recurrence, with the landmark proPSMA trial establishing its diagnostic superiority over conventional imaging; whether PSMA-PET-guided management improves long-term oncologic outcomes, however, remains an open question addressable only by prospective PSMA-specific trials. On the therapeutic side, 177Lu-PSMA-617 has become a standard treatment option for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) after androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) and taxane chemotherapy, and is moving into earlier lines of disease. Alpha-emitting and next-generation ligands, together with quantitative whole-body imaging and artificial intelligence, are redefining both patient selection and response assessment, although randomized evidence for many of these approaches remains limited. In Japan, the concurrent 2025 approval of 177Lu-vipivotide tetraxetan and its companion PSMA diagnostic has initiated a national roll-out that will depend on a hub-and-spoke framework of regional PSMA-PET centers and therapy spokes, a prepared nuclear medicine workforce, and domestic registries to refine Japanese-specific evidence. This review summarizes the current clinical evidence for PSMA-PET/CT and 177Lu-PSMA radioligand therapy, highlights interpretive and implementation pitfalls, and outlines practical priorities for the Japanese clinical and academic community.

title: DiffUltra: Task-Guided Pathology Synthesis for Large-Scale Real-World Lung Ultrasound Data
desc: Despite their scale, large medical imaging datasets may underrepresent clinically relevant pathological presentations. Synthetic data can expand coverage, but findings must remain compatible with surrounding anatomy. This is challenging in ultrasound, where findings resemble surrounding tissue and must be positioned relative to anatomical landmarks. We propose DiffUltra, a task-guided latent diffusion pipeline that models pathological structure and spatial context, and screens synthetic images for downstream utility. DiffUltra conditions generation on structural masks decomposing findings into anechoic, hypoechoic, and hyperechoic subregions. Two placement strategies insert findings into pathology-absent backgrounds or replace existing findings with structurally matched pathology from other patients. A filter trained exclusively on real data retains images whose predictions agree spatially with target boxes. We evaluate DiffUltra for lung ultrasound detection of pleural effusion and consolidation, using over 700,000 expert-annotated frames from 598 patients at 12 sites. Averaged across three real-data scales, synthetic insertion significantly improved video-level AUROC for both pleural effusion (p = 0.017) and consolidation (p < 0.01). For pleural effusion, frame-level average precision improved by 4.5 percentage points on average and by 6.1 points using only 10% of real data (p < 0.01 for both). Synthetic insertion also yielded larger average precision gains than an existing diffusion-based lesion-insertion method at every scale. At full scale, targeted synthesis improved AUROC for both pathologies by 1.1-3.9 points in an underrepresented anatomical zone and on a held-out acquisition system. These results suggest that anatomically constrained, task-guided synthesis can help address coverage gaps in ultrasound training data.

title: HIMSSCast: Breaking down the details of the HTI-5 final rule

Advanced cannabidiol delivery platforms: smart biomaterials, controlled release systems, and 3D-bioprinted therapeutic technologies.
desc: [Journal of drug targeting] Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid derived from Cannabis sativa L. has gained significant attention in biomedical research due to its broad spectrum of therapeutic properties, including anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, neuroprotective, and anticancer activities. However, its clinical translation remains limited by poor aqueous solubility, low bioavailability, rapid metabolism, and instability under physiological conditions. To overcome these challenges, advanced drug delivery platforms based on 3D bioprinting technologies have emerged as promising strategies for controlled and site-specific delivery of CBD. This review provides a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art CBD delivery systems, including polymeric biomaterials such as PLGA, PEG derivatives, chitosan, alginate, and cellulose-based hybrids, which enhance drug stability and enable sustained release profiles. Nano- and microstructured systems, including liposomes, nanoparticles, nanoemulsions, microspheres, and electrospun nanofibers, are discussed for their ability to improve bioavailability and facilitate targeted delivery at the cellular level. Hydrogel-based platforms, particularly injectable and stimuli-responsive systems, are highlighted for their role in localised therapy and tissue engineering applications. Furthermore, the integration of 3D bioprinting technologies enables the fabrication of patient-specific scaffolds and implantable constructs for precision medicine and regenerative therapies. Stimuli-responsive systems, including pH-, temperature-, enzyme-, and externally triggered release platforms, further enhance on-demand drug release in diseased microenvironments. The biomedical applications of CBD-based systems are critically evaluated in antimicrobial therapy, wound healing, tumour-targeted cancer therapy, immunomodulation, microbiome regulation, and regenerative medicine. Finally, this review addresses current translational challenges such as drug loading efficiency, stability issues, scalability, and regulatory barriers, while highlighting future perspectives involving artificial intelligence-guided design, personalised nanomedicine, and advanced biomanufacturing technologies. Overall, CBD-based smart biomaterial platforms represent a highly promising approach for next-generation therapeutic systems with improved efficacy, safety, and clinical potential.

title: BABA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Patient-Advocacy Agents
desc: An LLM agent that helps a patient get care must do two things. It must reach the correct outcome, and it must follow the necessary procedure. For example, the agent must get the patient's permission before it shares the patient's records. We introduce BABA-Bench, a benchmark of 47 interactive worlds. We built each world from a de-identified, real patient advocacy case that expert advocates reviewed. In each world, the agent must find hidden information and coordinate insurers, clinics, suppliers, pharmacies, and community organizations. The engine checks each action at the time the agent does it. It checks if the agent has permission, if the agent has evidence for the action, and if the action is prohibited. We evaluated 14 frontier models with three runs on each world, for a total of 1,974 runs. Agents often reached the correct outcome by an invalid route. Of the 921 runs that reached all required outcomes, 254 (28%) did not follow the necessary procedure. Claude Opus 5 reached all required outcomes in 81.6% of its runs, but only 52.5% of its runs passed all checks. When we gave two models a verified route, their pass rates increased from 29.8% to 91.5% and from 44.0% to 97.2%. For these models, the main problem is to find a route, not to execute it.

title: Deals channel feed
朗玛信息：扩大ToB医疗机构覆盖范围，推动AI医疗业务成为公司新的增长引擎
Beyond the Balance Sheet: Tangible and Intangible Return on Investment in Radiology Artificial Intelligence Adoption.
source: PubMed · Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR
desc: [Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR] Artificial intelligence (AI) products for radiology are being cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) at a pace that has outrun the field's ability to evaluate them financially. Hospital leadership, radiology directors, and other members on AI governance committees are routinely asked to justify high upfront and recurring costs using a return-on-investment (ROI) vocabulary built for capital equipment with a direct revenue line - a vocabulary that fits only a minority of the products now on the market. This paper argues that AI product ROI, when properly assessed, is not limited to departmental cash flows and must include both tangible value (billable revenue, throughput, avoided cost) and intangible value (diagnostic confidence, workforce retention, referring-physician trust, institutional reputation, and strategic optionality). This paper also reasons that the balance between tangible and intangible value is not constant across AI products or timelines. Instead, this balance shifts somewhat predictably with the underlying technology architecture and its associated use case, from narrow triage tools with fast, mostly tangible payoffs to platform and language-model products whose value is more diffuse and harder to separate from the surrounding workflow. Lastly, this paper proposes a governance framework - anchored by a proxy-measurement table that operationalizes both tangible and intangible value across eleven institutional domains - to help radiology leadership evaluate tangible and intangible ROI together at the point of purchase and track how each is expected to move across the product's operating life, ensuring deployment and renewal decisions are judged against realistic expectations for each individual AI technology for its specific use case.

title: Nedimo: An Evidence-Grounded Multilingual Pipeline for AI-Generated Sleep Stories
desc: Generative audio systems can produce large libraries of personalized bedtime content, but ordinary media objectives (retention, completion, and novelty) are poorly aligned with the goal of supporting a transition toward sleep. Direct evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, and a recent active-controlled trial did not support such audio as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance. We translate this uncertain evidence into conservative engineering requirements and present a multilingual pipeline for generating and narrating low-arousal sleep stories. The implemented prototype separates deterministic planning from large language model generation, represents content and delivery parameters explicitly, shapes each script through a four-phase attention taper, validates structural and lexical constraints, performs a bounded error-aware retry, and quarantines unresolved outputs. Provider-agnostic text-to-speech synthesis is followed by paragraph-aware joining, two-pass loudness normalization, and a publication gate that re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range, and true-peak limits. The product data model records stop position, replay, early abandonment, and completion while treating these events as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. We contribute an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria, and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. No clinical efficacy is claimed; the system is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool whose benefit and possible reliance must be evaluated empirically.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiogram Screening for Detection of Low Ejection Fraction in Routine Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
source: PubMed · Annals of noninvasive electrocardiology : the official journal of the International Society for Holter and Noninvasive Electrocardiology, Inc
desc: [Annals of noninvasive electrocardiology : the official journal of the International Society for Holter and Noninvasive Electrocardiology, Inc] Left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) is common and treatable but often undiagnosed, especially in early stages with non-specific symptoms. AI applied to standard ECGs offers low-cost screening for low ejection fraction (EF), yet its real-world impact on diagnosis remains unclear. A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs assessed AI-ECG screening for low EF in clinical practice. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261287652). Databases (PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Central, Google Scholar) were searched from inception to January 18, 2026, for RCTs comparing AI-ECG screening to usual care in adults without known heart failure undergoing routine ECGs. The primary outcome was new low EF (≤ 50%) confirmed by echocardiography. Secondary outcomes included echocardiography referral rates, positive predictive value, and cardiology referral rates. Pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs were calculated using a random-effects model. Three RCTs were included (two individual and one cluster) with 37,467 participants. After adjusting for clustering, AI-ECG screening significantly improved detection of new low EF diagnoses compared to usual care (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.64; p = 0.002; I2 = 0%), with a number needed to screen of 204. No significant difference was found in echocardiography referral rates (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.09; p = 0.55; I2 = 36%). The PPV of the AI tool ranged from approximately 20% to 34% across studies. AI-ECG screening added to routine care improves low EF detection without substantially increasing echocardiography referrals. These findings support AI-ECG for earlier LVSD detection in at-risk populations, though further validation across diverse AI platforms is warranted.

title: Report-Derived Labels, an Image Teacher and the Gap to Expert Labels in Knee MRI: An Analysis of One Entry to the RSNA 2026 Knee Abnormality Detection Challenge
desc: In the RSNA 2026 Knee Abnormality Detection challenge, 58 of 4,407 training studies have expert labels for 12 findings, and the rest have only a radiology report. We compare training targets built from a language-model reading of the reports and from a public image model against two references: the expert labels and the 39,248 study-finding cells that the reports state as present or absent. The report labels and the out-of-fold predictions of the image model reach similar agreement with the expert labels (macro AUC 0.892 and 0.896) but fail on different findings. The report is better for ligament tears and patellofemoral osteoarthritis, which it never calls present when the experts do not; the image model is better for effusion, Baker's cyst, contusion, and synovitis, where the reports call the finding absent, leave it out, or call it present more often than the experts. Their equal mixture reaches 0.927 (gain over the report labels 0.035, 95% interval 0.019 to 0.052), also after removing the studies whose knee side was handled inconsistently. We did not observe a model-level gain from this better target: a 2.5D ResNet50 trained on the report labels alone scored 0.877 on the private leaderboard, after the deadline, against 0.872 for the same model trained on the mixture, and the out-of-fold advantage of the mixture is confounded by a change of code and by possible leakage through the image model's folds. A scanner prevalence prior raised agreement with the reports but not with the experts, so a report-derived reference can reward reporting habits. A rank correction for co-occurring findings gave small out-of-fold gains and no visible leaderboard effect. Our entry, a forked public ensemble with that correction, was displayed at rank 582 of 6,299 on the private leaderboard (0.943, a score shared by 287 teams). All results are exploratory; none of the models is meant for clinical use.

title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)-Based Review of RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction Methods.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) play a vital role in cellular processes including gene regulation, RNA editing, and translational control. Aberrant RRIs are increasingly recognized as contributors to cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis. Accurate computational prediction of RRIs therefore offers significant opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, understanding tumor biology, and therapeutic target identification. Among machine learning approaches, support vector machines (SVMs) have been applied in RRI prediction due to their robustness in handling high-dimensional, nonlinear data and relatively small training datasets. This chapter reviews SVM-based methods for RRI prediction, highlights representative tools and strategies, and discusses current challenges and relevance to cancer application. Emerging trends that integrate SVMs with deep learning and experimental data augmentation are also outlined, pointing toward pathways for clinical translation.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Expert-Assisted Interpretation of Histopathology Foundation Model Embeddings
desc: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Three-Dimensional Preoperative Planning for Total Knee Arthroplasty in End-Stage Knee Osteoarthritis​.
source: PubMed · Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE
desc: [Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE] Accurate preoperative templating for total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in patients with end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA) remains challenging, and the accuracy of conventional planning methods is variable. This preliminary, retrospective, single-center study evaluated the reliability of a robot-independent, artificial intelligence (AI)-based, three-dimensional (3D) preoperative planning system (AIKNEE) for predicting prosthesis size and component position in patients undergoing TKA for end-stage KOA. Twenty-eight knees from 24 patients with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 3-4 KOA were included. The primary outcome was the agreement between the planned and implanted prosthesis sizes. Secondary outcomes included correction of the coronal hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle, improvement in Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) knee scores, and early postoperative complications. The planned size matched the implanted size exactly in 53.57% of femoral components (15/28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 35.8%-70.5%) and 46.43% of tibial components (13/28; 95% CI, 29.5%-64.2%). Agreement within ±1 size was 85.71% for femoral components (24/28; 95% CI, 68.5%-94.3%) and 96.43% for tibial components (27/28; 95% CI, 82.3%-99.4%), giving an overall matching rate of 91.07% (51/56; 95% CI, 80.7%-96.1%). The postoperative HKA angle improved from 173.0° ± 3.9° to 178.2° ± 1.2° (P < 0.001), and the HSS score increased from 39.7 ± 2.2 preoperatively to 80.8 ± 1.3 at the 1-month follow-up (P < 0.001). No major early complications, including infection, dislocation, or deep venous thrombosis, were observed. Within this preliminary cohort, the AIKNEE system predicted prosthesis size with a reliability comparable to that reported for existing AI templating tools. Because the study was retrospective, single-arm, unblinded, and limited to 1 month of follow-up, these data characterize planning accuracy only and do not demonstrate clinical effectiveness; adequately powered, controlled studies with long-term follow-up are required.

title: PathoJev: Efficient Pathology Decisions from Shared Visual Context
desc: Pathology workflows require multiple visual judgments about the same slide, from identifying tumor type to assessing grade and invasion. Generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions. Building on the System One paradigm, we introduce PathoJev, a pathology model that directly predicts answer probabilities for whole-slide and region-level assessment. PathoJev encodes each slide once and evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context. Reusing the hybrid backbone's recurrent states further limits the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question. Across three whole-slide benchmarks, the 9B and 27B models achieve mean accuracies of 77.2% and 78.1%, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points. Both scales also maintain competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks. On WSI-Bench, the 9B model runs 9.1x faster than SlideChat. Shared context accelerates eight-question workloads by 6.9x and 5.9x over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2x and 8.9x for 64 questions. These results provide a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment. Code: https://github.com/ChyaZhang/PathoJev.

title: Artificial intelligence attitudes, presenteeism, and work engagement among nurses: a structural equation modeling approach.
desc: [Frontiers in psychology] The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has transformed clinical practice, yet the psychological mechanisms linking nurses' AI attitudes to their occupational functioning remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the role of presenteeism as a potential explanatory pathway. This study aimed to examine the relationships among nurses' attitudes toward AI, presenteeism, and work engagement, and to test the mediating role of presenteeism within a Job Demands-Resources framework. A cross-sectional correlational design was employed, with data collected from 806 hospital nurses across Saudi Arabia and Egypt using the AI Attitude Scale for Nurses, the Presenteeism Scale in Nursing, and the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale. Data were analyzed via structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation testing (2,000 resamples) and multi-group invariance analysis. Following the exclusion of four multivariate outliers, the final analytic sample comprised 802 nurses. The hypothesized model demonstrated good fit (CFI = 0.981, RMSEA = 0.068). AI attitude significantly and negatively predicted presenteeism (β = -0.366, p < 0.001) and positively predicted work engagement (β = 0.436, p < 0.001), while presenteeism negatively predicted engagement (β = -0.250, p < 0.001). Presenteeism significantly and partially mediated this relationship (indirect β = 0.092, 95% CI [0.065, 0.123]), with the model explaining approximately 33.2% of variance in engagement. Configural, metric, and structural invariance was confirmed across Egyptian and Saudi nurses. These associational findings suggest that more favorable AI attitudes are linked to lower presenteeism and stronger engagement, offering preliminary guidance for nursing management and healthcare digitalization policies pending longitudinal confirmation.

title: Cross-Device Transfer of a Hospital-Trained Fetal Head Circumference Model to a Low-Cost Handheld Ultrasound Probe
desc: Automated fetal head circumference (HC) measurement reaches near-expert accuracy on the HC18 benchmark, but published models are trained and evaluated on hospital-grade equipment. We quantify what happens when such a model is carried to a low-cost handheld probe. A lightweight segmentation network (CSM, 0.13M parameters) was trained on HC18 across five independent runs and applied without modification to images from a $1,350 handheld probe (SonoQue C3), acquired at the same visit as the reference hospital scan in 18 patients. In-domain accuracy was 2.34 +/- 0.43 mm; on handheld images the same model gave 16.12 mm against the hospital record, a 6.9-fold degradation. Input preprocessing, a choice rarely reported, accounted for about a third of that gap: direct resizing gave 49.45 mm against 16.12 mm for an aspect-preserving pipeline. A leave-one-out data-efficiency curve showed that fine-tuning on two images significantly worsened accuracy, and that from four images upward error fell by 0.75 mm per doubling of the local dataset (p = 0.0045), although no training-set size up to 27 images significantly improved on the unmodified model. Much of the residual gap belongs to the reference rather than the model: scored against a manual tracing of the same image the model was already within 10.48 mm, and its disagreement with sonographer calipers on the same frame was a near-constant offset, negative in 10 of 10 cases. A single calibration constant estimated leave-one-out reduced that disagreement from 8.12 mm to 3.49 mm, reaching the intraobserver reproducibility reported for experienced sonographers, but did not improve agreement with the hospital record. Cross-device evaluations should therefore report the input preprocessing used and characterise the precision of their reference standard.

title: Artificial Intelligence-powered Advances in Phytomedicine: A Systematic Review on Plant-based Drug Discovery Software.
desc: [Current drug discovery technologies] Herbal medicines contain complex phytochemicals that offer therapeutic potential, but their long-term adverse effects remain challenging to determine. Traditional herbal medicine preparation methods are often labor-intensive, non-standardized, and face difficulties in identifying active ingredients. By improving medication development, optimization, and discovery procedures, Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides innovative ways to get beyond these restrictions. This systematic review aims to evaluate the role of AI-based software such as LEAFSNAP, Deep- Chem, PlantNet, Autodock, MestReNova, XCMS, ADMETlab, SynergyFinder, KEGG, TCMID, and Reactome in enhancing phytomedicine research by streamlining plant identification, bioactive compound discovery, molecular modeling, and pharmacokinetic profiling, thereby advancing drug discovery and development processes. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA guidelines) to explore the integration of AI-based tools in phytomedicine research and drug discovery. Literature searches were performed in Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases, focusing on studies published between January 2015 and January 2025. Only English-language articles focusing on AI-based software for drug discovery from plant-derived compounds were reviewed. Studies discussing synthetic drug development were excluded; this, along with non-English language, acted as a literature review limitation. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the retrieved articles. Any discrepancies in the screening, study selection, and data extraction processes were resolved through discussion and consensus. Through the effective identification of bioactive chemicals and the simplification of intricate studies, the combination of artificial intelligence and computer tools has completely transformed the process of discovering and developing herbal drugs. Artificial intelligence tools like ADMETlab for pharmacokinetics and toxicity assessments, DeepChem for molecular activity modelling, and AlphaFold for protein structure prediction have greatly improved the search for new herbal drugs. While AutoDock improves molecular docking simulations by automating ligand-receptor binding predictions for bioactive chemicals, LeafSnap and PlantNet make plant identification simpler. Drug development workflows are improved by databases such as KEGG and TC

title: TheseusSyn: Unified Medical Image Synthesis via Context-Conditioned Masked Autoregression
desc: High-fidelity medical image synthesis is promising for data-efficient learning and privacy-preserving model development. However, most existing approaches rely on symbolic or label-based conditioning, which constrains generative diversity and limits case-specific contextual fidelity. Inspired by the Ship of Theseus paradox, we propose TheseusSyn, a novel context-conditioned synthesis paradigm that generates images through iterative content replacement. Our framework employs a multi-codebook discrete tokenizer to convert medical images into sequences of token indices, extracted with a global representation token that serves as a contextual constraint. A masked autoregressive generative model then iteratively masks and predicts tokens conditioned on both local neighborhoods and the global context. By progressively replacing image content until the entire token sequence is renewed, TheseusSyn produces synthetic samples that preserve anatomical coherence and semantic consistency while introducing controlled diversity. We evaluate the proposed framework on multiple datasets from MedMNIST by constructing synthetic datasets with varying masking strategies and training ResNet-18 classifiers exclusively on either real or synthetic data. Experimental results demonstrate that classifiers trained on TheseusSyn-generated images achieve competitive performance on official test sets, indicating that the synthesized data preserve diagnostically relevant features and semantic consistency. Systematic analysis of masking strategies reveals their impact on structural fidelity and downstream classification accuracy. These results suggest that context-conditioned masked autoregression provides an effective and generalizable solution for label-free medical image synthesis, offering a scalable alternative to conventional data augmentation and class-conditioned generative models in medical imaging applications.

title: Artificial intelligence in axial spondyloarthritis imaging: a review of current evidence.
desc: [Current opinion in immunology] The diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) remains challenging and is frequently delayed. Imaging is central to diagnosis, but relevant inflammatory and structural abnormalities may be subtle, heterogeneous, or overlap with findings related to mechanical stress, anatomical variation, and degeneration. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is therefore being investigated to support image interpretation, lesion detection, quantification, and standardized assessment. We synthesize evidence from 12 studies applying convolutional neural networks and related architectures to magnetic resonance imaging and radiographs, automate imaging scores, and combine imaging-derived information with clinical variables. Several models achieved performance comparable to experienced human readers, including during external validation. However, performance may decline in heterogeneous real-world populations for study-specific reasons not explained solely by scanner or protocol differences. No AI tool currently has regulatory clearance for autonomous use in axSpA, and applications remain largely confined to research and clinical trials.

title: Single-Annotation, Multi-Hypothesis Segmentation with Semantic-Spatial Residual Banks
desc: Multi-rater segmentation datasets show that a single image can admit several valid masks, yet most training sets expose only one annotation per image. We study single-annotation multi-hypothesis segmentation: each training image exposes one fixed mask, while the model must return a finite bank that covers held-out human annotations at test time. Our experiments reveal a representation tradeoff. Banks learned directly from images recover variations in local boundaries and extent but lose structural hypotheses, whereas frozen semantic features preserve structural grouping but underrepresent spatial variation. We introduce the Semantic-Spatial Residual Bank (SSRB), which freezes a semantic bank trained with balanced assignments and learns a residual from the image for each hypothesis. Across five medical endpoints, SSRB improves coverage of held-out masks at $K=8$ over a Probabilistic U-Net under the same one-mask constraint. On LIDC and LIDC-hard, it also produces substantially more distinct useful masks. On BSDS, it preserves the semantic bank's performance in grouping regions. Its advantage grows as more masks are returned, showing that residuals learned for corresponding heads improve coverage of local annotation variation while preserving how regions are grouped.

title: From CYP450 pharmacogenomics to personalized medicine: clinical evidence, dosing guidelines, and future perspectives.
desc: [Pharmacogenomics] Interindividual variability in drug response remains a critical challenge in contemporary pharmacotherapy, and cytochrome P450 (CYP450) genetic polymorphisms are a principal determinant of this heterogeneity. The CYP450 superfamily mediates the oxidative biotransformation of 70-80% of clinically prescribed medications. Genetic variants in key isoforms generate four distinct metabolizer phenotypes, producing up to 1000-fold interindividual differences in drug clearance that directly translate into therapeutic failure, adverse drug reactions, or life-threatening toxicity. This review critically synthesizes current mechanistic, clinical, and translational evidence on CYP450 pharmacogenomics, emphasizing genotype-guided individualized dosing across anticoagulation, antiplatelet therapy, oncology, neuropsychiatry, and solid organ transplantation. Guidelines from the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group, the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium, and the FDA are evaluated alongside phenotype-specific dosing algorithms. Emerging approaches are examined, including model-informed precision dosing, Bayesian pharmacokinetic forecasting, next-generation sequencing for haplotype resolution, and artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support. Persistent barriers, including phenoconversion by drug-drug interactions, under-representation of populations in pharmacogenomic datasets, and inconsistent guideline adoption, are critically appraised. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for relevant literature published between 1978 and 2026. Coordinated global integration of CYP450 genotyping into routine clinical workflows is needed to advance the transition from reactive to preemptive, genuinely personalized pharmacotherapy.

title: CSF cytology: core principles, diagnostic pitfalls and emerging digital tools including artificial intelligence and telecytology.
desc: [Acta neuropathologica] Cerebrospinal fluid cytology remains a cornerstone of diagnostic evaluation in infectious, autoimmune, haemorrhagic, and neoplastic disorders of the central nervous system despite advances in neuroimaging, molecular diagnostics, and digital technologies. This narrative review summarises established principles of cerebrospinal fluid cytology, highlights methodological limitations and diagnostic pitfalls, and integrates emerging developments, including automated cell counting, artificial intelligence, and telecytology. Pre-analytical factors are critical determinants of diagnostic accuracy. Delayed sample processing promotes pH-dependent autolysis and substantial cell loss, whereas rapid cytocentrifugation preserves cellular morphology and facilitates reliable assessment. Automated cell counters are increasingly implemented in routine laboratories and offer advantages in settings with limited technical staffing. However, current systems show limited precision in samples with low and slightly elevated cell counts and limited morphological evaluation. Manual chamber counting, particularly in the normal and low-cell-count range, remains the gold standard for quantitative CSF cell assessment, whereas expert microscopic examination remains the reference standard for qualitative cytomorphological assessment. Although the sensitivity of neuroimaging continues to improve, cerebrospinal fluid cytology retains a unique diagnostic role in the detection of infectious and neoplastic conditions and in the evaluation of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Cytological detection of erythrophages, siderophages, and haematoidin crystals can reveal haemorrhage and provide clues to its temporal stage. Overall, cerebrospinal fluid cytology remains a valuable diagnostic tool when integrated with clinical, laboratory, microbiological, immunological, and imaging findings. Careful recognition of common pitfalls is essential. We recommend rapid cerebrospinal fluid processing, routine preparation of cytospin-based stained slides with expert microscopic review, and the implementation of automated or digital methods only within clearly validated workflows.

title: The diversity of artificial intelligence in dentistry: Toward more sustainability?
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)
desc: [Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)] Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming policy, research, education, and the practice of dentistry through advances in diagnostics, treatment planning, education, and administration. Despite its clear potential in service delivery and care and transdisciplinary collaboration, the adoption of AI remains fragmented and uneven. The landscape of AI applications in dentistry spans diverse users, tasks, and contexts and presents challenges as well as opportunities for sustainable integration. Moving beyond the typical focus on diagnostic accuracy, the authors investigated dental and medical studies, analyzing how AI can remain sustainable across the profession's fragmented and heterogeneous ecosystem. Some key barriers, such as siloed innovation, ethical uncertainty, and unequal infrastructure, are identified and suggest the need for cohesive engagement across stakeholder groups and collective actions, development of curriculum and ethical frameworks, and regulatory initiatives. The authors outline strategic steps to leverage the profession's diversity as a driver of sustainability.

title: Artificial intelligence-guided design of high-entropy materials from bulk to nanoscale.
desc: [Nanoscale advances] High Entropy Materials (HEMs) have provided a breakthrough in materials science, moving beyond single-principal-element design to multielement (>5) design with multiple elements in near-equiatomic ratios. This compositional complexity introduces high configurational entropy, stabilizing single solid-solution phases and providing outstanding thermal, mechanical, and functional characteristics to alloys, oxides, carbides and nitrides. Although traditional empirical methods are the cornerstone of materials design, they are less efficient in exploring the vast compositional and processing space in the sphere of HEMs. The recent development of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has altered the field of HEM research by allowing data-driven prediction of phase stability, structure-property relationships, and processing results, which has tremendously accelerated the process of materials discovery. With the combination of thermodynamic descriptors, including, but not limited to, ΔS mix, mixing enthalpy (ΔH mix), atomic size mismatch (δ), phase purity (Ω), and valence electron concentration (VEC), AI models enable researchers to perform composition and property optimization more easily than ever before. The AI-guided frameworks, despite their limitations like the lack of data, can enable autonomous and high-throughput design of HEMs. This viewpoint reflects recent developments, examples of energy and catalytic processes, and the future outlook and the potential transformative nature of AI to provide next-generation high performance entropy-stabilized materials.
